episodes.title: Episode 04: The other half of the turn
notes: Decisions per game (both players): 246 with 2+ options; buys 54 (22%), action plays 106 (43%), gains (Artisan/Remodel/Workshop) ~7 with 10-13 options
None of 748 (c2 buy -> alternative) pairs over 430k positions beats c2 beyond chance: gains are rare, position-specific
Action teacher only: 56.2% vs c2 (200 games, 95% interval 51.5-60.8%), changed 229 of 10,187 action decisions
Changes: 160 other action, 69 stop instead of play, 0 play instead of stop
Combined buy + action teacher: 62.0% vs c2 over 300 games (95% interval 57.3-66.3%)
transcript: You asked a sharp question. Are we only looking at buys? What about playing actions, the order you play them in, and the choice to buy nothing or play nothing? The honest answer was yes. So far we only looked at buys. This episode is about what happened when we looked at the rest.

First, I counted. I played two hundred games of our best model against itself. I recorded every decision with two or more options. A game has about two hundred and forty six of them, counting both players. Buys are only fifty four. That is about one in five. Playing actions is the biggest group, about one hundred and six per game. Then come smaller ones, like what to trash with a Chapel, what to discard to a Militia, and what to gain with an Artisan or a Remodel. Those gains are really buys in disguise, with ten or more options each.
Buying nothing was already covered. The teacher always tests passing as one of its choices. But playing nothing was not. When to stop playing actions was left entirely to the best model.

Second, I looked for the reason the small network stopped improving. I took about four hundred and thirty thousand graded buys. Then I asked a simple question many times. When the best model bought card X, would card Y have been better, on average? I tested seven hundred and forty eight such pairs. Not one of them beat the best model by more than chance. That is a strong result. The best model has no simple buying mistakes, like always taking a Silver where a Market is better.

So where do the teacher's wins come from? From rare exceptions. In a few percent of positions, the exact deck, supply and score make a different buy better. Each graded buy is noisy, much noisier than those small gains. So the small network sees mostly noise, and it has stayed at about fifty percent for many rounds. That is why I paused it.

Third, the experiment. I built an action teacher. It works just like the buy teacher, but at action decisions. When the best model is about to play an action, the teacher tries every legal option, including stopping. It plays each one to the end of the game, thirty two times, on the same shuffles. It only changes the choice when the gain is clearly larger than the noise. Because it is asked again at every action, it also decides the order.

The result surprised me. On actions alone, with the best model doing all the buying, the teacher won fifty six percent over two hundred games. The uncertainty range runs from about fifty one to about sixty one percent. That is as large as the gain from buys.

And it changes very little. It graded about ten thousand action decisions and changed only two hundred and twenty nine. That is about two in a hundred. Most of those changes, one hundred and sixty, played a different action. Sixty nine stopped where the best model would have played on. And not once did it play an action where the best model wanted to stop. So the best model's habit is to play too much, not too little. That fits what you see in Dominion. Playing a terminal action can draw a dead hand or use up your one action, and sometimes it is better to keep it for later.

What does this mean? Our best model was built for one decision at a time, without looking ahead. Looking ahead with full replays fixes a few of its choices in both phases of the turn. Each fix is small, but they add up to several percent of win chance.

Then I ran a combined teacher, grading both buys and actions. It played three hundred games against the best model, and won sixty two percent. The uncertainty range runs from about fifty seven to about sixty six percent. So the two gains really do add up. That is the strongest Dominion player this project has measured.

There is a catch, as always. It is slow, because every graded decision costs a few hundred replays. Next, the plan is to make the teacher faster. And to find a better way to teach a small network these rare exceptions. One idea is to spend many more replays on fewer positions, so that each lesson is clear.

episodes.title: Episode 03: Making the teacher twice as fast
notes: Profile first: the network was 83% of teacher time, the game rules under 3% (the floor, about 30x max)
Sparse, transposed forward pass: 2.85x per move in C, 1.6x in Rust (float reordering lets C vectorise)
End to end 2.2x: 62 -> 137 rollouts/s per process; labels ~5 -> 10.7 per second
Exactness: 1,000 of 1,000 games identical with the fast code
Workers spawned fresh: memory from ~940 MB each to 356 MB in all; why a GPU would not help (batch 1, serial)
transcript: This episode is for engineers who are learning machine learning. You asked whether we could speed up training with Rust, or with something else that is fast. We did get it twice as fast. But the interesting part is how we found out where the time went, and why the obvious answer was the wrong one.

First, a quick reminder of what is slow. The teacher grades every buy by playing the game to the end. It tries about six buys, and each buy gets sixteen to thirty two replays. That is a couple of hundred whole games, just to label one decision. And in every one of those games, our best network makes every single move.

Rule one of speeding things up is this. Measure before you change anything. The engine was already written in C, so you might guess the game rules are the slow part. They are not. I built a small stand alone program that plays a few teacher games, and ran it under a profiler. A profiler samples where the program is, many times a second, and adds it up per function. The answer was clear. Eighty three percent of the time went into one small function. It multiplies the network's weights by its inputs. The game rules took less than three percent.

That three percent matters. It is the floor. Even if the network cost nothing at all, the rules would still take three percent of the old time. So the best you could ever hope for is about thirty times faster. Engineers call this Amdahl's law. A speed up is limited by the part you do not touch.

So the job was the network. It is small. Four hundred and thirteen numbers go in. They pass through two layers of two hundred and fifty six units, and thirty four scores come out, one per possible choice. That is about one hundred and eighty thousand multiply and add steps per move. And it runs one position at a time. In machine learning terms, that is batch size one.

Here is the first lesson for anyone coming from deep learning. Most of the inputs are zero. When I counted them on real recorded positions, only about one hundred and twenty four of the four hundred and thirteen were not zero. Most cards are not in this kingdom. Most zones are empty. And after the first layer, about half the hidden units are zero too. The activation function sets every negative number to zero. Multiplying by zero is wasted work.

So I rewrote the multiply. First, I flipped the weight table, so that each input owns one long row of weights. Then, for each input that is not zero, the code adds that whole row into the hidden layer. The processor can do that eight numbers at a time. Zero inputs are skipped completely. The same trick works for the second layer. And during a replay, we only need the scores of the moves that are legal right now. We never need the value estimate at all. So those get skipped too.

Then came the bake off you asked for. I wrote the same new method in C and in Rust. Then I timed both against the old code, on the same four hundred recorded positions. The old code took about fifty five microseconds per move. The new C code took about nineteen. That is almost three times faster. Rust took about thirty five, so it was only one and a half times faster.

Why did Rust lose? It is not a slow language. The difference is a promise about arithmetic. With floating point numbers, the order of additions changes the last few bits of the answer. The C code here is compiled with a flag that says, you may reorder my sums. That lets the compiler split one long sum into eight sums that run side by side. Rust never reorders sums unless you write the code to do it. Same algorithm, different rules about rounding. So the language matters much less than the algorithm and the compiler flags.

Rule two. Prove that the fast version is the same game. Changing the order of additions changes the scores in about the fifth decimal place. That could flip a near tie, and then a game would go differently. So I played one thousand games both ways, old code and new code, with the same seeds. All one thousand came out identical: the same winner, the same score, the same number of turns. The labels in the benchmark games matched exactly too.

Rule three. Measure end to end, not one part. The network got almost three times faster. But the whole program only got two point two times faster, because the parts that did not change now take a bigger share. Replays went from sixty two per second to one hundred and thirty seven, in one process. Graded buys went from about five per second to almost eleven.

There was a second, quieter win, in memory. The label workers were copies of the training process. Each one carried almost a gigabyte, including the whole data set and the deep learning library. On a laptop with seven gigabytes, that is how training gets killed. Now each worker starts fresh, and all five together use about three hundred and fifty megabytes.

And what about a graphics card? This laptop does not have a usable one. But even with one, it would not help much. A graphics card is fast when you give it thousands of positions at once. Here every move depends on the move before it, one position at a time. That work is serial. More processor cores would help almost directly. A bigger graphics card would mostly wait.

What is next? The profile now says the network is two thirds of the time, and building its inputs is more than a quarter. The weights are also slightly too big for the processor's fastest cache, so the network is now limited by memory, not by arithmetic. Those are the next targets. Meanwhile, the teacher result is confirmed on kingdoms it had never seen. It won fifty five percent against the newest version of our best model, over four hundred games. Against the older version it is near fifty nine percent so far. And the small fast network now gets twice as many lessons per hour.

episodes.title: Episode 02: The teacher beats our best model
notes: Gated teacher (32 paired draws, gain > 2 SE and > 0.02): 56.2% vs c2 2654, 59.4% vs c1 2300 (160 games each, intervals above 50%)
It overrides about 4-5% of buys; ~1 s per buy
Student after 49.6k labels: dev regret 0.059 vs c2 0.047; dev score ~50%
Next: teacher confirmation on 200 reserved kingdoms vs c2 and c1
transcript: Last time, the teacher lost. It played our best model and won only about forty one percent of the games. It kept changing good buys on the strength of a lucky replay.

So I gave it one rule. It may only change the best model's buy when the gain is clear. The gain has to beat two standard errors of the measurement, and it has to be at least two points. Each choice now gets thirty two replays instead of sixteen.

With that rule the teacher changes only about one buy in twenty-five. And it wins. Against the newer version of our best model it scored fifty six percent over one hundred and sixty games. Against the older version it scored fifty nine percent. In both cases the uncertainty range stays above fifty percent. Those are the first numbers that beat the third reinforcement learning network.

Why does it work? The best model is very good, but it makes a few buys that it would regret if it could see the whole game play out. The teacher plays out each choice to the end, with the best model's own play afterwards, and keeps only the changes that clearly pay.
The catch is speed. The teacher needs about one second for each buy, because it plays a couple of hundred games in its head. For a game on Steam that is fine. For training and big tests it is slow.

That is why the small, fast network is still training. It has now seen about fifty thousand graded buys. It is learning, but slowly. Its picks still lose a little more value than the best model's own picks, so for now it almost never overrides. Its test games sit right at fifty percent. Each buy label is noisy, and it needs many more of them.

Next, a bigger check of the teacher runs on two hundred kingdoms it has never seen, against both versions of the best model. And the small network keeps collecting about twenty thousand graded buys an hour. If it starts to copy the teacher's few good changes, we get the same gain in one fast step.

episodes.title: Episode 01: A challenger that prices every buy
notes: Teacher: paired rollouts to the end of the game for c2's top 5 buys + PASS
Gate 1: teacher on c2 scored 41.5% after 100 games vs c2 (noise: winner's curse)
Student round 1 on 2,118 labels: flat outputs; fixed to rank only graded candidates and read c2's preferences
Training now: 20,000 labels per round, dev match of 600 games each round
Goal: >= 53% vs RL-v3 c1 2300 and c2 2654 on 2,000 reserved kingdoms
transcript: You asked for a new model that could beat our best one. So tonight I started a new project. It asks a simple question. What is each buy actually worth?

Our best model today is the third reinforcement learning network. It wins about eighty six percent of its games against the genetic algorithm base. It plays every decision with one network. When it buys a card, it says what it would buy. It never says how much better that card is than the next one.

The new project tries to measure exactly that. At each buy, a teacher takes the best model's top five choices, plus buying nothing. It plays each one to the very end of the game. Every choice sees the same shuffles of the hidden cards, so the comparison is fair. After that, the best model plays every move for both sides. The share of games won is the price of that buy.

The teacher is slow. One game where it grades every buy takes about half a minute. So the plan is to teach a small, fast network to predict those prices. It looks at the cards in the kingdom as a set, and it scores every buy in one step.

Before any of that, I tested the teacher itself against the best model. It lost. After one hundred games it had about forty one percent. The reason is noise. With only sixteen to thirty two replays per choice, the teacher often thinks a card is better when it was just lucky. It changed the best model's choice on about one buy in five, and many of those changes were mistakes.

The small network has a second chance, because it learns from many positions at once. Luck in one position cancels out across thousands of them. The first small network was trained on only two thousand positions. It learned nothing useful yet. Its prices were flat, and it picked cards it had never been shown. I fixed two things. It now only chooses among the cards the teacher actually graded. And it gets to see the best model's own preferences, so it starts close to them.

Training is running now. It collects twenty thousand graded buys per round, which takes about an hour on this laptop. After each round it plays six hundred test games against the best model. It only overrides a buy when it is confident by a margin.

What I expect is honest uncertainty. Buys differ by a few percent of win chance, and each label is far noisier than that. We probably need a hundred thousand positions or more before the network can see the signal. The goal is fifty three percent against both versions of the best model, on two thousand kingdoms it has never seen. If the dev games stay below fifty percent after a few rounds, I will say so, and we will look at why.
You can follow every round on the project site.
